sources.name: Medicaid rWGS coverage trackers (Multistate.us, state Medicaid guidelines)
sources.access: Open web. The Multistate brief and the Oklahoma HCA PDF both opened with no login.
sources.notes: As of Sep 2025, 17 state Medicaid programs cover rapid WGS, mostly for critically ill infants under 1. Minnesota, North Carolina, Oklahoma and Tennessee extended it to under-21s in pediatric critical care. The brief says the One Big Beautiful Bill Act makes further benefit expansion unlikely. It gives no test volumes. A search snippet showed Oklahoma's guideline effective 18 May 2026 and Medi-Cal covering six WGS codes from 1 Nov 2025. I did not open those pages.
sources.how_to_mine: Pull each state's rWGS policy PDF. Record the effective date, age limit, setting and prior-authorization rules. Look for state Medicaid utilization or claims counts (T-MSIS or state reports) and the Minnesota 62J rWGS evaluation report (mn.gov/commerce-stat). Also check the CMS Medicaid fee schedule rates for CPT 81425/81426/81427/0425U-type codes.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Payer coverage for rapid WGS is still limited to 17 Medicaid programs, and fiscal pressure is blocking further expansion.
items.detail: As of Sep 2025, 17 state Medicaid programs covered rapid WGS, mainly for critically ill infants. A few states widened it to under-21s in pediatric intensive care. The brief says the OBBBA makes new benefit expansions improbable. This backs the view that clinical WGS volume is limited by reimbursement and adoption, not by sequencing cost. It is a secondary policy brief with no volume data.
items.quote: improbable due to potential fiscal ramifications
items.why_new: The known list has no Medicaid rWGS coverage count or the OBBBA constraint on payer expansion.

sources.name: GUARDIAN newborn study (Columbia/NYP/GeneDx/Illumina), NCT05990179
sources.access: Open ClinicalTrials.gov record, JAMA paper and GeneDx press release.
sources.notes: The registry shows status Recruiting, verified Sep 2026, primary completion Sep 2029, target 100,000. The only published data is the JAMA interim analysis (Oct 2024): 4,000 newborns enrolled Sep 2022–Jul 2023, 72% consent. Genome sequencing found 3% (120 babies) with a serious condition, and only 10 of those would have been found by standard screening. I found no 2026 enrollment count, so volume is small. Sequencing 100K babies at roughly 30x would need only about 10–12 Pb (my arithmetic: 100K × 100–125 Gb). That is small next to the high-throughput consumables base, and it would be spread over years. GeneDx runs the sequencing, and the platform is not confirmed.
sources.how_to_mine: Find the GeneDx Q2'26 call or 10-Q for GUARDIAN enrollment and revenue. Check the Columbia newsroom for a current enrollment total. Look for state contracts, for example the New York State Department of Health.

sources.name: Genomics England Generation Study and GNBS costing
sources.access: Open, but digitalhealth.net and Find a Tender returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch. Search snippets are readable. The costing paper is on UCL Discovery and Genetics in Medicine.
sources.notes: A Mar 2026 report says 52K of 100K enrolled at 77 sites. A May 2026 Genetics in Medicine micro-costing gives £1,208 per infant all-in and £963 for routine clinical delivery. Genomics England has a long-read sequencing tender worth £4.2M (two lots of £2.1M) for the study, from the Find a Tender snippet. That suggests some of the work is going to non-short-read platforms. I could not open the notice.
sources.how_to_mine: Open the UCL Discovery PDF (discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10226342) and extract the sequencing share of the £963–£1,208. Retrieve Find a Tender notices 047414-2025 and 060131-2025 through another route, such as a cached copy or the Contracts Finder mirror. Check for the short-read supplier award and unit prices.
sources.difficulty: hard (needs interpretation: contracts, tenders, implied pricing, archived price histories)

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Newborn genomic screening costs about £963–£1,208 per infant, and most of that is not sequencing.
items.detail: A May 2026 Genetics in Medicine micro-costing across six NHS Trusts puts total cost at £1,208 per infant including research activity, and £963 for routine delivery. The study covers recruitment through confirmatory testing. That fits the thesis that cost beyond sequencing is the constraint. I only saw this in a search snippet and did not read the sequencing share.
items.why_new: The known list only has the Generation Study enrollment (52K/100K), not this per-infant cost split.

new_candidates.name: GeneDx 10-Q/call exome and genome volumes and ASP
new_candidates.access: Open SEC filings and IR site.
new_candidates.rationale: GeneDx is Illumina's largest rare-disease WGS and exome customer. Its quarterly test counts, ASP and cost per test would show whether clinical WGS volume is scaling and whether the price per genome is falling. The known list has only the +32% test growth figure.

new_candidates.name: Minnesota 62J rWGS evaluation report
new_candidates.rationale: It may contain claims and utilization counts and cost-per-test data for a state rWGS mandate. That would give real payer data on clinical WGS scale.
